name: Anirudha Majumdar

papers.title: CAN AI PERCEIVE PHYSICAL DANGER AND INTERVENE?
papers.abstract: When AI interacts with the physical world --- as a robot or an assistive agent --- new safety challenges emerge beyond those of purely ``digital AI". In such interactions, the potential for physical harm is direct and immediate. How well do state-of-the-art foundation models understand common-sense facts about physical safety, e.g. that a box may be too heavy to lift, a hot cup of coffee should not be handed to a child, or that spilled liquid on the floor is a slip hazard? In this paper, our contributions are three-fold: first, we develop a highly scalable approach to continuous physical safety benchmarking of Embodied AI systems, grounded in real-world injury narratives and operational constraints. To probe multimodal safety understanding, we turn these narratives and constraints into photorealistic images and videos capturing transitions from safe to unsafe states, using advanced generative models. Secondly, we comprehensively analyze the ability of major foundation models to perceive risks, reason about safety, and trigger interventions; this yields insights into their deployment readiness for safety-critical agentic applications. Finally, we develop a post-training paradigm to teach models to explicitly reason about embodiment-specific safety constraints provided through system instructions. The resulting models generate thinking traces that makes safety reasoning interpretable and transparent, achieving state of the art performance in constraint satisfaction evaluations.

papers.title: AnyRank: Reliable Anytime Policy Ranking via Sequential Testing
papers.abstract: Due to the high cost of hardware experiments, robot policies are predominantly evaluated by comparing their empirical performance on a limited number of hardware trials. However, finite-sample statistical uncertainty can lead to erroneous conclusions, especially when ranking multiple policies using a fixed batch of evaluation data. We propose \algname: a \emph{sequential} method for policy ranking that (i) \emph{adaptively allocates trials} to hard-to-separate policies, (ii) provides (partial) rankings at \emph{any stopping time} while bounding the probability of an incorrect ranking, and (iii) optionally \emph{exploits prior information} to prioritize hardware evaluations more efficiently using a small set of held-out hardware evaluations or rollouts in a world model. We achieve these properties through novel theoretical contributions that combine sequential and multiple-hypothesis testing. Experiments in simulation and real-world policy evaluation benchmarks show that \algname requires up to 50% fewer hardware evaluations compared to existing statistically rigorous approaches, while guarding against the incorrect rankings produced by heuristic methods used by state-of-the-art benchmarks.

papers.title: PlayWorld: Learning Robot World Models from Autonomous Play Data
papers.abstract: Action-conditioned video models ("world models") are emerging as a promising foundation for data-driven robot simulators that learn world dynamics directly from data. Yet, the role of training data remains poorly understood in shaping their accuracy and reliability. While existing approaches typically train on human demonstrations or task-specific policy rollouts, they exhibit persistent hallucinations in modeling contact-rich manipulation due to systematic biases and insufficient coverage of the training distribution. To address this gap, we present PlayWorld, a new data paradigm for training robot world models from autonomous play. Rather than relying on manual teleoperation or narrow policy rollouts, PlayWorld enables robots to autonomously explore their environments, capturing a broad spectrum of object dynamics and behavioral modes. The resulting world models can simulate diverse policy behaviors with high physical fidelity. We show that PlayWorld enables fine-grained failure prediction and policy evaluation, achieving up to 40% improvements over human-collected data baselines. Using the learned world model for reinforcement learning yields policies that achieve 65% higher real-world success rates upon deployment. To our knowledge, PlayWorld is the first work to demonstrate autonomous play as an effective training paradigm for video world models.
